newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean bankers arrested in growing loan scandal.
newsitem.headline: South Korean bankers arrested in growing loan scandal.

text.p: Prosecutors arrested two leading bankers Wednesday and a prominent politician said he had taken money from the man at the centre of a loan scandal involving the Hanbo Group.
A prosecution spokesman said Sheen Kwang-shik, president of Korea First Bank, and Woo Chan-mok, head of Cho Hung Bank, were arrested on charges of bribery and taken to a Seoul jail.
Prosecutors accused Sheen and Woo of taking 400 million won ($460,000) each from Chung Tae-soo, founder of the troubled Hanbo Group, in return for huge loans from the two banks.
The move follows the arrest Friday of Chung, who was still being questioned by prosecutors on whether he provided kickbacks to other bankers or politicians, senior prosecutor Choi Byung-koog said.

Korea First and Cho Hung, along with the state-run Korea Development Bank, are the main creditors of Hanbo Steel, which racked up about five trillion won ($5.8 billion) in loans before it was declared insolvent Jan. 23.

In a fresh twist to the scandal, lawmaker Kwon Roh-kap, a close associate of opposition leader Kim Dae-jung, said he had accepted between 150 million and 160 million won ($173,000 and $184,000) from Chung, partly to fund an election campaign.
Kim Dae-jung, who heads the main opposition National Congress for New Politics, has accused the government of peddling influence for the massive loans to Hanbo Steel.

Asked by reporters Wednesday about the nature of the money he received from Chung, Kwon said: "I believe they were either political funds or rice cake money. But I have nothing to do with preferential lendings to Hanbo."
South Koreans traditionally swap small amounts of money, known as rice cake money, or gifts during major holidays as a token of friendship or respect.
Kwon said part of the money was used to finance a party election in 1993.

He is the first politician to admit taking money from Chung, who built up South Korea's 14th largest conglomerate by rapidly expanding the steelmaking flagship and acquiring or setting up 18 companies over the past three years.
